messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Inspector
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Downward Comparison: I remind myself it could have been worse, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Ravi Patel is a 42-year-old tax inspector who lives with his wife and two children in a suburban town outside Chicago. He came to therapy at his wife's urging, after months of what she called "disappearing inside himself." Ravi described the incident with a flat, quiet voice, as though he were reading a report he had already memorized: eighteen months ago, while driving to a rural business audit, he glanced down to adjust the GPS and struck a motorcyclist who had stopped at a crossroad. The man—forty-three, a father of three—suffered a traumatic brain injury and spent weeks in intensive care. Ravi did not know the outcome for certain; he assumed the worst, and he had never allowed himself to look up the man's name or condition. What he remembered instead were fragments: the sound of the motorcyclist's helmet scraping across the asphalt, the way the man's hand flopped open as he lay on the road, the high-pitched ringing that seemed to come from inside Ravi's own skull afterward. Some moments were impossibly clear—the pattern of the man's denim jacket, the exact angle of the bicycle's bent wheel—while other parts of the sequence, like the actual impact, were completely blank. That blankness haunted him more than the clear images. He could not trust his own memory, and it made him feel as though he had never properly understood what happened, as if he had escaped into a white fog while someone else's life ended.

In the weeks and months that followed, Ravi developed a set of convictions that he never spoke aloud but that governed his days. He had come to believe that he was permanently humiliated—not because anyone had shamed him, but because he knew the truth about himself: he was the kind of person who could ruin a stranger's family while adjusting a GPS. His belief that the world was basically orderly and that good people were protected had shattered completely. He had always seen himself as careful, law-abiding, a public servant who followed the rules. After the accident, he felt like a fraud. He told himself he deserved to suffer, and he found a grim comfort in that punishment thinking, because at least it gave him a reason for his constant dread. He also caught himself thinking, "At least he didn't die," or "It could have been worse—he might have been a child," but these downward comparisons brought no relief; they only reminded him that he was bargaining with his own conscience.

Ravi tried not to think about the event. He suppressed the memories with a fierce, silent effort, but they broke through anyway. Certain sounds triggered auditory recall: a car horn, the screech of tires, a motorcycle engine idling at a traffic light—he would hear the scrape of the helmet across the pavement again, sometimes for hours afterward. He avoided driving past the intersection where it happened, took long detours that added twenty minutes to his commute. When his supervisor scheduled a team meeting to discuss a case involving a road-rage citation, Ravi claimed a migraine and left early. Funerals and cemeteries became unbearable. When a coworker's father died and the office sent a condolences card, Ravi could not bring himself to sign it; he left it on the break room table and walked away. He knew this was irrational—the dead man in the funeral home was not the motorcyclist—but the grief in the air felt like an accusation, as if all mourning belonged to him.

His work suffered. A tax inspector must examine receipts, cross-check figures, catch discrepancies. Ravi, who had once been meticulous, now found himself reading the same line three times without comprehension. He stopped offering to do fieldwork, citing vague "medical appointments," and stayed in the office reviewing files that required no travel. His wife noticed his withdrawal. He stopped attending his daughter's soccer games because the field bordered a cemetery. He stopped driving the family to weekend trips. His wife asked what was wrong, and he said "Nothing, I'm just tired." He believed he did not deserve her concern, and he felt that if she knew the full extent of his humiliation, she would see him as a monster.

What finally brought Ravi to therapy was a morning in late September when he saw a news report about a car hitting a pedestrian. He stood frozen in his kitchen, the coffee growing cold in his hand, and heard the motorcyclist's helmet scrape again. His wife found him there, pale and silent, and she told him he had to get help. Ravi came to the first session with his shoulders bowed, expecting judgment. He told the therapist he was not sure anything could help, and that the only thing he hoped for was to stop feeling so afraid of his own mind. He did not say it aloud, but what he feared most was that the man he had injured had died, and that Ravi's own life would always be measured against that death—a debt he could never repay.
